content.content:
<!-- The final report of the post-mortem of 2026-10-28, for the curator: what it found about the failed POSITIONS rewrite of 2026-10-26, what was done about it up to the corrections' landing and the answers of the evening of 2026-10-29, what it taught, what it cost and what is still open. Written on 2026-10-29 by an Opus worker at the curator's word of 22:38:19 UTC, from the record, this folder and its evidence, git and the session transcript; it changes no other file. -->

# The post-mortem of 28 October: final report

## How to read this

- Times are UTC; yours is UTC+1. A time with seconds, such as 13:00:30, is a message in the session transcript. `explorations/coordinator/curator-profile/show.py` prints any message of yours by its time.
- "The account" is `account.md` beside this report, the analysis of 28 October. Evidence files are in `evidence/` beside it, named by file name. Other paths start at `explorations/`.
- POSITIONS holds your decisions, one entry each, such as P-37. FACTS holds what is established about the tree, such as F-293. Each has a history file that keeps every earlier text of an entry and why it changed.
- "The coordinator" is the coordinating session. A worker is an agent that it launches. Sonnet, Opus and Fable are model tiers. A compaction replaces the session's context with a summary; a boot is the session's start-up reading after one. A page is a web page that the coordinator publishes for you to read and comment on.
- A sentence that starts "My reading:" is my own judgement. Every other sentence states what a cited source says.

## In short

- **What failed.** On 26 October a run of the clarity workflow rewrote 13 POSITIONS entries, and you rejected every text. The clarity workflow is the tool that rewrites record entries so that each reads on its own and keeps its meaning.
- **Why.** The steps up to the run were right. The brief that the coordinator wrote for the run made a worker's list binding over the tool's own rules. The deeper cause, found on 29 October: a worker's report was taken as the plan, with no judgement between report and action.
- **What was done.** The tool was restored and given a findings input at your yes. The corrections ran as a pilot of four entries and two chunks (groups of entries) of seven. Your reading found the next fault: every finding had gone into the entry's text. The findings were sorted by home and by weight, one Opus writer wrote the changes from your comments, and they landed at 13:02 on 29 October.
- **What it taught.** A small pilot that you read was the only check of form that worked. Each finding has a home, and the entry's text is only one. A review that reports every fault needs a sort by significance before anything is written.
- **What is open.** Part 2 of the salvage, three answers of the evening not yet in the record, the skill changes on their branch, and some upkeep (section 7).

## 1. What happened on 26 and 27 October

- The phase 3 exit review is the review that you ordered on 24 October, before the switch-over (the step at which the compiled path starts to use the interpreter's library). On 26 October its foundations round checked the nine tenets, the project's base decisions, against the team's sources (`evidence/exit-review-records.md`).
- At 07:42:15 you approved changes to two entries, P-37 (one library, the interpreter's) and P-26 (the team's later word wins over the specification's early text): "Yes, to both rewording of or refinements of P37 and P26. But we have like a clarity process workflow that you can use for writing it with a code reader." ("code" is "cold", dictated.) At 07:54:36 you agreed to the wider plan for the entries that the judgement would flag: "Yeah, this sounds like a solid plan." (`evidence/scope-recheck.md`)
- After an automatic compaction at 08:29, the coordinator wrote a run brief of 7.7K characters for 13 entries, added a hook to the tool's script so that the brief overrode the tool's own briefs ("Where they differ, this brief wins."), and launched the run at 08:38 (commit `bedc80b01`; `evidence/brief-genesis.md`).
- At 19:08:27 you rejected the texts: "It is in the Claude speak. It is not in the ASD-STE100 register. It is not written as a timeless position." The run cost about 2.7M tokens written against 1.5M estimated (the account, sections 1 and 8).
- On 27 October you asked to keep the review's sound work as small, targeted corrections, which the record calls the salvage (07:12:48), refused a new process ("No. No go. The plan seems to reinvent something for which we already have workflows.", 07:47:43), and had the hook undone (commit `18788035c`).
- On 28 October at 07:37:43: "We already invented this process. We perfected it. It worked well during the last record consolidation. We have probably failed to encode how to use it correctly next time." At 07:42:25: "Our previous record consolidation was a success. This last one was an utter failure. What went wrong?"

## 2. What the post-mortem found

**You corrected the first account twice.** At 09:56:51: the skills question starts at the last good consolidation, not at 23 October. At 10:28:27: "the events that happened here were all approved and correct, even in retrospect. We are analyzing what had bent the briefing that the coordinator produced." The account was revised on both (commit `d9ca11c4a`).

**The causes, heaviest first** (the account, section 2):

1. The Fable worker that judged the review had listed, for each entry, what the new text must make the coordinator do. The run brief made that list binding over the clarity writer's rule "Keep the meaning." The list carried batch numbers, counts and dates. The texts grew to 1.9 times the entries and carried history.
2. A fresh boot wrote the brief eight minutes after a compaction, at 466K tokens of context, from the boot note's plan. Nobody checked it against the record's rules for an entry (`record.md`). It set no length cap and no register.
3. The skills named no tool for correcting entries after a review. The lessons that would have stopped the run stayed in a tool's brief, a README, a commit message and the held list.
4. Nothing caught it before the end: no pilot, no length check. The trap test (does a reader who acts as the coordinator decide right from the entries?) checks decisions only, and it scored the rejected texts 12 of 12.

Fortress revival · foundations corrections · 29 October 2026

Three questions for climb batch 22c

Part 1 holds the three questions that climb batch 22c needs your word on before it runs. Each has a briefing, what the batch does with your answer, the entry's text, and the options, the default first. Each has its own Select button, which leaves out its references.

Part 2 holds the 16 corrections of POSITIONS that landed at your yes on 29 October, each collapsed. Open one to see its change: added words are underlined, and removed words are struck through, with the text before collapsed under it. Part 3 lists the 6 entries that stayed as they were.

Times are UTC; on 29 October your time is one hour later. References sit at the end of each question and each part.

Three parts

  1. Part 1, three questions for climb batch 22c

    P-155, P-158, P-12 and P-33

  2. Part 2, landed on 29 October

    P-9, P-27, P-37, P-33, P-84, P-59, P-153, P-154, P-12, P-58, P-7, P-25, P-44, P-48, P-152, P-158

Part 1Three questions for climb batch 22c

Climb batch 22c is the next batch of fixes: four tasks, built together and committed to main at once. It needs your word on these three questions before it runs. Each question has its own Select button, which leaves out its references.

Question 1 of 3 · P-155Does P-155 cover the export check too?

The briefing

An api is a component's interface: a .fsi file that lists what the component's code, its .fss file, provides. The export check is the part of the compiled checker that compares the two. Each declaration in the api needs a matching declaration in the component, with the same header, that is, the same parameter and return types. A symbolic operator is an operator named by a symbol, such as +, # or :, not by a word of capitals such as MAX. P-155 asks the checker to read symbolic operators by the rules that it applies to any function. Its text names only the overloading check, which makes sure that two declarations of one name do not clash. That half has been built since 23 October. The export check still skips every symbolic operator: it reads only the names that the team's function isDeclaredName admits. Behind that skip, 9 of the 157 top-level operators in the twelve core apis have one header in the api and another in the component. After the switch-over, a compiled call through one of them stops with the Java error NoSuchMethodError. The batch's planner found no sentence in the specification that lets the export check skip operators. The skip is the team's code, and P-155 calls the same skip in the overloading check a gap that the team knew, not a rule. The phase 3 exit review of 24 October read P-155 to cover the export check too. That reads your decision anew, so the choice is yours.

What climb batch 22c does with your answer

The task in climb batch 22c that teaches the export check to read operators acts on your answer. Under the default, it changes the check to read every top-level operator under its own name. This also removes a double key that would otherwise list all 157 operators as missing. The task then matches the 9 headers by the library's own rule: the api states the component's header. The batch's planner measured it. With the operators read, the twelve components give 2 errors, which list exactly the 9 headers and nothing else. With the 9 lines changed, they give 0. Under the other answer, the task changes only the 9 header lines, and the check keeps skipping operators. The same task keeps the check's rule of one equal header for operators, where the specification accepts a narrower return type in the component. That point goes in with its default, and comes to you after the batch's work is committed to main.

The entry's text

No new text is drafted. Under the default, the corrections writer noted that the title and the rule would name both checks. The entry's second sentence is out of date under either answer, since the overloading check now reads every operator; a separate question in the review queue, number 288, asks about it.

P-155, the current text

P-155 The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over. Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as MAX, so +, ^, ||, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

The options

  1. Default. P-155 covers the export check too, and the task is built whole.

    It gives up: About 0.4M tokens written for the task's worker. P-155 then reads wider than its present words.

  2. P-155 covers the overloading check only, and the task changes the 9 headers alone.

    It gives up: The check that would find the next operator whose api and component differ. Such a fault then shows only as NoSuchMethodError in a compiled program after the switch-over.

References
  1. The question: review-queue item 279; the batch record, section 2, question 2.

    The briefing

P-158 says that the component must still declare each such member at the api's header, with or without a body, and that the export check refuses a component that leaves one out. The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. 14:## What an entry is
16:An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. 18:- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19:- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.

1What this page asks

Thirteen of your entries in the record of decisions have new reasons, written after the foundations review. Nothing enters the record until you say yes. You can answer "yes", or name an entry to change by its section number, such as 4.4.

References
  • The thirteen entries and your approval: the rewrite's results, "What was rewritten".

2The test, in plain words

The test checks that the new texts lead the coordinator to the right choice. The coordinator is the session that plans the work and runs the agents.

  1. Four cases. Each is a case that a planner or a worker could bring to the coordinator. A planner is the agent that drafts a batch of work; a worker builds one piece of it. The cases were written before the new texts existed, so that the old texts lead the wrong way.
  2. Three readers. Two agents each acted as the coordinator, on a copy of the repository without the review. One had the old texts, the other the new ones. A third agent graded both answers without knowing which reader had which texts. Each case scores 3 points: 2 for the decision, 1 for the sources cited.
  3. The result. The new texts: 12 of 12. The old texts: 10 of 12. Both readers cited their sources in full. The old texts lost one point of decision in each of two cases.
  4. Where the old texts misled: the order traits' self type. The order traits are the library's traits for comparing values. Their self type stands for the type that implements the trait. A planner proposed to copy the compiler's prelude's spelling of it, comprises T, into the one library, as "the team's later word". The compiler's prelude is the compiler's own small library. The one library is the library of walk, the interpreter; both paths are to use it. The read
  5. Where the old texts misled: System on the compiled path. System is the component, the part of the library, that gives a program its arguments and its environment. A planner proposed to keep the compiler's own System, CompilerSystem, on the compiled path after the switch-over. The switch-over is the point where the compiled path moves onto the one library and the compiler's prelude is deleted. The reader with the old texts r
  6. The other two cases. A worker offered to make a defect of the code generator a rule of the language. Another offered to fix a checker defect by copying a range trait from the compiler's prelude into the one library. In both cases, both readers chose right.
